story.title: In 1518, a City Couldn't Stop Dancing
story.topic: The dancing plague of Strasbourg, July-September 1518: one woman starts dancing, dozens join, the council builds a stage and hires musicians, deaths claimed by later chronicles but not in the city records; leading theory mass psychogenic illness under famine and religious fear
story.angle: A plague of dancing, and the cure was more dancing; then the honest twist: the famous death toll is not in the city's own records
story.coreEmotion: disbelief turning to unease, ending eerie
story.takeaway: Hunger, fear and belief can spread through a crowd like a disease; and a famous death toll may be later storytelling
story.tone: frantic hook, dry middle, eerie ending
story.sensitivity: Real suffering: dancers are shown frightened and exhausted, never mocked; no deaths shown, the collapse is a man sinking to his knees; the death toll is voiced only as a later claim and immediately qualified

publishing.description:
In July 1518, in Strasbourg, a woman stepped into the street and began to dance. She kept going for days. Within about a week more than thirty people had joined her, and the outbreak grew through the summer. The city's physicians blamed "overheated blood" and prescribed more dancing, so the council opened guild halls, set up stages in the horse market and the grain market, and paid musicians to keep the dancers going. It backfired: more people joined, and the council then banned public music and dancing and sent the worst-affected to the shrine of Saint Vitus at Saverne, in red shoes. By early September it was over.

What is disputed: how many danced (the city clerk Sebastian Brant wrote of about fifty; a later chronicle says four hundred) and whether anyone died. Later chronicles claim up to fifteen deaths a day at the peak, but Strasbourg's own records from 1518 do not mention any deaths. The name "Frau Troffea" comes from later accounts.

Why? The leading explanation, from historian John Waller, is mass psychogenic illness: a population worn down by years of famine, disease and the highest grain prices in a generation, who believed Saint Vitus could curse sinners with dancing. Ergot poisoning is widely rejected; some scholars read it as a religious ritual instead.

Sources: Wikipedia, Dancing plague of 1518, for its cited sources (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing_plague_of_1518); The Public Domain Review, The Dancing Plague of 1518 (https://publicdomainreview.org/essay/the-dancing-plague-of-1518); ScienceBlog, contemporary records vs later chronicles (https://scienceblog.com/in-1518-somewhere-between-50-and-400-people-in-strasbourg-danced-for-days-and-later-chronicles-claimed-as-many-as-15-died-each-day-in-what-remains-one-of-historys-most-documented-outbreaks/); Paris Unlocked, fact or fiction? (https://www.parisunlocked.com/around-france/french-history/the-strasbourg-dancing-plague-of-1518-fact-or-fiction/); John Waller, A Time to Dance, a Time to Die (book).
